Described in this chapter are Carboprost, p.2006 Meteneprost, p.2010 Dinoprost, p.2006 Misoprostol, p.2013 Dinoprostone, p.2007 Sulprostone, p.2018 Gemeprost, p.2010 Tocolytics Tocolytics inhibit uterine contractions and are used in pre- mature labour to delay early delivery. Beta agonists other than ritodrine have also been used, and details on salbuta- mol (p.1131) and terbutaline (p.1138) can be found in the chapter on Bronchodilators and Anti-asthma Drugs. Other drugs that have been tried for their tocolytic actions in- clude calcium-channel blockers (see Nifedipine, p.1350), glyceryl trinitrate (p.1296), magnesium sulfate (p.1679), and NSAIDs (see Indometacin, p.66). Described in this chapter are Atosiban, p.2005 Ritodrine, p.2017 Management of Obstetric Conditions The management of some obstetric conditions is dis- cussed below. Labour induction and augmentation The uterus is normally spontaneously contractile but dur- ing pregnancy various physiological mechanisms main- tain it in a quiescent state; retention of the fetus is also aid- ed by a firm and contracted cervix. During the final 4 to 5 weeks of pregnancy the cervix normally undergoes a ‘ripening’ process in which it becomes softened and dilat- ed, so that at parturition it is not a barrier to delivery of the fetus. Endogenous prostaglandins play an important role in this process, and also sensitise the uterus in preparation for labour. • Labour usually begins spontaneously but in some cases it may be necessary to induce labour, for example in pregnancies that go beyond term or where rupture of the membranes occurs without labour. In other cases there may be indications for early delivery such as maternal hypertensive states, antepartum haemorrhage, intra- amniotic infection (chorioamnionitis), or intra-uterine fetal death.1,2 • Once labour has started, augmentation of uterine activi- ty may be necessary if contractions fail to progress sat- isfactorily. A process of active management of labour, including early oxytocin augmentation, has been used in nulliparous women with a single fetus presenting head- first at term and showing no evidence of fetal compro- mise. Although it may shorten labour without increas- ing maternal or neonatal harm, it has not been shown to reduce the rate of caesarean section.3 Various techniques are available for induction of labour, and the choice may be influenced by the ripeness of the cervix and whether the membranes are intact or have rup- tured.
